x.why: When someone asks AI about a store's return period or delivery cost, the answer comes from these pages. Rules hidden in a PDF, a pop-up or dense legal text are harder for AI to read and quote correctly.
x.how: Check that each policy has its own HTML page linked from the footer. Rewrite legal wording into short sentences with concrete numbers, such as days and costs. Make sure the numbers match the feed and the structured data. Done when all four pages exist, are indexable and give the same numbers as the feed.

items.t: Authors and E-E-A-T

x.what: E-E-A-T stands for experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness, the qualities Google's guidelines use to judge content quality. In practice, each article shows a named author with a short bio, linked to an author page that describes their real experience, for example years as a photographer or store adviser.
x.why: Google and AI tools give more weight to content from people whose experience is visible and checkable. Anonymous store text is harder to trust.
x.how: Create an author page for each regular writer with name, role, experience and links to their profiles elsewhere. Show the author and the date on every article. Done when all articles have a named author linked to an author page.

items.t: Data nobody else has
items.d: Sample photos, in-store tests, popularity rankings.

x.what: Content only this store can publish: sample photos taken with the gear it sells, results of tests done in its own stores, popularity rankings based on its own sales. A manufacturer spec sheet looks the same on every site, while this data exists in one place only.
x.why: The AI can choose from many copies of the same spec sheet, so it has no reason to cite one particular store. Unique data gives it a reason to quote this store as the source.
x.how: Pick one or two kinds of own data to start, for example sample photos for the top lenses or a monthly bestseller list per category. Publish them on product and category pages with the date and how the data was gathered. Done when the chosen data is live on the pages and updated on a fixed schedule.

items.t: Freshness
items.d: Quarterly review and after launches, update date plus dateModified.

x.what: Guides, buying-choice pages and key descriptions are reviewed every quarter and after major product launches. Each page shows a visible updated-on date, and the structured data carries the same date in the dateModified field (the date of the last real change).
x.why: Photo and video gear changes fast, and AI tools use dates to judge how current a page is. A guide that still calls last year's model the newest leads to wrong answers.
x.how: Keep a list of pages with an owner and a next review date. After each review, update the content, the date shown on the page and dateModified, and change the date only when the content really changed. Done when every page on the list was reviewed within the last three months and the shown date matches dateModified.

items.t: Title and meta description for real queries, without the price

x.what: The title is the page name shown in the browser tab and as the headline in search results. The meta description is the short summary shown below it. Both use the words people actually search for, such as the model name and product type, and neither includes the price.
x.why: Search and AI systems use these fields to understand what a page is about. A price in the description goes out of date and can still be shown as the current price long after it changed.
x.how: Use Search Console to see which searches lead to each important page, and write the title and description with those words. Remove prices from all meta descriptions and from the templates that generate them. Done when a check with an SEO crawler (a tool that scans every page of the site) finds no prices in meta descriptions.

items.t: Glossary of 100-200 terms

x.what: A glossary of 100-200 photo and video terms explained in plain words, such as IBIS, crop factor, rolling shutter or ND filter. Each entry has a short definition, an example and links to related products and guides.
x.why: People ask AI what technical terms mean while choosing gear. A clear definition on the store's site can be quoted, and its links lead from the term to products.
x.how: Take terms from the bank of questions and from the product spec fields. Write a short entry for each term and have an adviser check it. Link the terms from product pages and guides. Done when the glossary has at least 100 terms, each on an indexable page or section.

items.t: Images: many angles, descriptive alt, readable file names, WebP or AVIF

x.what: Each product has several photos from different angles: front, back, top, ports, with lens and without. Each image has an alt text that describes what it shows, for example 'Sony A7 IV body, rear view with tilting screen'. File names are readable words instead of random codes. Images are saved in WebP or AVIF, modern formats that load faster than JPEG at the same quality.
x.why: AI systems cannot look at a photo the way a customer does, so they rely on alt text, file names and the text around the image. Good descriptions let them match your images to questions about a specific model, and fast images keep pages quick for both people and crawlers.
x.how: Pick 20 top product pages. Check that each has at least 4 angles, a specific alt text on every image and a file name with brand and model. Check in the browser's network tab that images load as WebP or AVIF. Fix the image template so new products get this by default. Done when the sample passes and new uploads follow the rule.

items.t: IPTC metadata on own photos
items.d: Creator, Credit, Copyright.

x.what: IPTC metadata is information stored inside the image file itself: who took the photo, who should be credited and who owns the copyright. This item applies to photos your own team makes, such as sample shots from cameras, store photos and studio product photos. Fill in at least the Creator, Credit and Copyright fields.
x.why: Search engines and AI tools can read this data and show who made an image. It helps your own photos stay linked to your brand when they are reused or shown in image results, and it documents your rights if a licence question comes up.
x.how: Agree one standard text for Creator, Credit and Copyright. Add it as a preset in the photo editing or export tool your team uses, so every exported file carries it. Check by opening 10 recently published own photos in a metadata viewer. Done when all of them show the three fields.

items.t: Video with transcript and captions, VideoObject, YouTube channel

x.what: Product videos, reviews and tutorials come with a full text transcript and captions. On your site, each video page carries VideoObject, a piece of structured data (code that describes the page to machines) with title, description, thumbnail, length and transcript. Videos also live on a maintained YouTube channel under your brand.
x.why: AI assistants read text much better than they watch video, so a transcript turns a video into content they can quote. VideoObject tells search engines exactly what the video is, and YouTube is one of the sources AI answers often draw on.
x.how: List your published videos. Add captions and a transcript to each, on YouTube and on the page where the video is embedded. Add VideoObject to those pages and test them in Google's Rich Results Test. Done when every new video ships with captions, transcript and valid VideoObject, and the YouTube channel links to your site.

items.t: Customer photo gallery (with consent)

x.what: A gallery where customers share photos they took with gear bought from you, for example sample shots from a lens shown on its product page. Each photo is published only with the customer's clear consent, with a record of who agreed and to what.
x.why: Real sample photos are content that no other store has, and they show what a product does in real use. Unique material of this kind gives AI systems a reason to cite your page instead of a copy of the manufacturer's text.
x.how: Decide where the gallery appears, for example on product pages for lenses and cameras. Ask your lawyer for consent wording covering publication and licence. Set up a simple upload or submission route with moderation. Done when the gallery is live on at least one product group and every photo has a stored consent.

items.t: Brand Facts Document
items.d: One document with the official facts about the company, the source for all profiles.

x.what: A Brand Facts Document is one internal document with the official facts about your company: legal name, founding year, addresses, phone numbers, opening hours, services, awards, social profiles and key numbers. It is the single source that every listing, profile and press text copies from.
x.why: AI systems compare what many sources say about a company and repeat what they agree on. If your facts differ between sites, the AI may give customers wrong hours or addresses, or trust you less. One master document is the way to keep every source the same.
x.how: Write the document in a shared place with one named owner. Include every fact that appears on your site and external profiles. Add a date of last review. Done when the document exists, an owner is named and the team uses it when updating any profile.

items.t: Same company data everywhere
items.d: Name, addresses, phones, hours, services on the site, Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, comparison and review sites, social. Compare 5 sources per store.

x.what: Your company name, addresses, phone numbers, opening hours and services read the same everywhere: your website, Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, price comparison and review sites, and social profiles. Small differences count, such as an old phone number or different holiday hours.
x.why: AI assistants build answers from several sources at once. When sources disagree, they may show the wrong data or skip your store in local questions such as 'where can I try this camera near me'.
x.how: For each physical store, compare the data in 5 sources against the Brand Facts Document (10.1). Note every difference in a simple table and fix it at the source. Repeat after any change of hours or address. Done when all 5 sources match for every store.

items.t: Google Business Profile for every physical store

x.what: Every physical store has its own verified Google Business Profile, the free listing that appears in Google Maps and local search. The profile has the correct address, hours (including holiday hours), phone, categories, photos and a link to the matching store page on your site.
x.why: Google uses these profiles in AI Overviews and AI Mode when people ask where to buy or test gear nearby. A missing or outdated profile means your store does not appear in those answers.
x.how: Log in to Google Business Profile and list all your locations. Check that each store has a verified profile and that every field matches the Brand Facts Document (10.1). Add holiday hours before each holiday period. Done when every store is verified and complete.

items.t: Reviews on independent platforms with steady volume
items.d: KPI: reviews in the last 90 days per platform.

x.what: Customers leave reviews about your store on independent platforms, such as Google, Trustpilot and local price comparison or review sites. The aim is a steady flow of new reviews every month, without long gaps after a single campaign. The measure is the number of reviews in the last 90 days on each platform.
x.why: AI assistants check what independent sources say about a store before recommending it. Recent reviews on outside platforms show that real customers buy from you now, and your own site cannot provide that proof.
x.how: Choose the platforms that matter in your country. Send a review request after delivery or pickup, through the platform's own invitation tool where it has one. Track reviews from the last 90 days per platform in your monthly report. Done when the KPI is reported every month and no main platform goes a month without new reviews.

items.t: Real delivery time matches the promised one

x.what: The delivery time you promise on the product page, in the feed and in structured data matches the time customers actually wait. If a page says 'delivery in 24 hours', most orders should arrive in 24 hours.
x.why: AI systems read your delivery promise and repeat it to customers. If reality is slower, customers complain in reviews, and those reviews feed back into what AI says about your store.
x.how: Take a sample of recent orders and compare the promised delivery time with the actual one, per delivery method. Where the gap is large, change the promise or fix the process. Repeat the check every quarter. Done when promised and actual times match for most orders in the sample.

items.t: Awards shown with the reason they were given
items.d: Plus award in Organization.

x.what: Awards and ratings your store has received are shown together with the reason: who gave the award, when and for what, with a link to the source. A badge alone says less than a short line explaining it. The award is also listed in the 'award' field of the Organization structured data on your home page.
x.why: AI systems prefer facts they can check. An award with a source and a reason can be verified and repeated in an answer, while a logo image on its own gives them nothing to read.
x.how: List your current awards. For each, add a sentence with the awarding body, the year, the reason and a link to the announcement. Add the awards to the Organization structured data. Done when every award shown on the site has its reason and source, and the structured data lists them.

items.t: Experts active in communities
items.d: Photo forums, Reddit, YouTube: real help, no ads.

x.what: Your staff experts take part in photo forums, Reddit, YouTube comments and similar communities. They answer questions, share tests and explain technical topics, with no sales pitches or links pushed into every post. The company agrees an approach first: who takes part, where, and how they say they work for you.
x.why: AI assistants draw heavily on community discussions when answering buying questions. Helpful answers from known experts build a reputation that AI models pick up and connect with your brand.
x.how: Choose 2-3 experts and the communities where your customers ask questions. Write a short guideline on tone, disclosure of employment and what not to post. Set a regular time budget. Done when the guideline exists and the experts post helpful answers every month.

items.t: PR based on own data

x.what: Press work built on data only you have, for example the most popular lenses of the year from your sales, trends in used camera prices or what customers ask most in your stores. You publish the findings on your site and offer them to journalists and bloggers.
x.why: Media and bloggers who quote your data link back to you, and AI systems treat such mentions as independent sources. Original data is also hard for competitors to copy.
x.how: Pick one data set you can publish without revealing confidential numbers. Write a short report with charts on your site. Send it to relevant photo and tech media. Done when at least one data-based story is published and you track who picked it up.

items.t: Wikidata and Wikipedia only from independent sources
items.d: sameAs in Organization.

x.what: Wikidata is a free public database of facts that many AI systems use, and Wikipedia is the encyclopedia built on similar rules. Your company may have entries there only if they are based on independent sources such as press articles. You do not write promotional entries yourself. Your Organization structured data links to these entries through the 'sameAs' field, which tells machines that both describe the same company.
x.why: AI models rely on Wikidata and Wikipedia to identify companies. A correct entry helps them know who you are, while a promotional entry is likely to be removed and can harm your reputation.
x.how: Check whether entries about your company exist. If they do, check facts against the Brand Facts Document (10.1) and suggest corrections through the talk pages with sources. Add the links to 'sameAs' in the Organization structured data. Done when existing entries are correct and linked.

items.t: Waiting lists joined, availability in your country tracked
items.d: Google UCP and Business Agent, chatgpt.com/merchants, Copilot Checkout, Perplexity.

x.what: Several AI platforms are building ways to buy directly inside the chat: Google UCP and Business Agent (through Merchant Center), the ChatGPT merchant programme at chatgpt.com/merchants, Copilot Checkout and Perplexity. Most of them start in the USA. This item means signing up to their waiting lists and checking regularly when they open in your country.
x.why: When a programme opens in your market, stores already on the list can join early. Stores that wait may miss the first period when competition inside AI shopping is still low.
x.how: Sign up to each programme's waiting list or interest form. Write down the date and the contact. Check each programme's status every quarter and note changes for your country. Done when you are on every available list and someone owns the quarterly check.

items.t: Meeting with the payment provider about agent payments
items.d: Agent tokens, local methods for agents, timeline, fraud liability.

x.what: A meeting with your payment provider about how AI agents will pay. Topics: agent tokens (a way to let an agent pay with a customer's saved method without seeing card details), which local payment methods will work for agents, the provider's timeline and who carries the cost of fraud in agent purchases.
x.why: An AI agent can only finish a purchase if your payment setup accepts its way of paying. Knowing your provider's plans early tells you when agent sales become possible for your store.
x.how: Book a meeting with your payment provider's account manager. Prepare the four topics as questions. Write a short note with their answers, dates and open points. Done when the note exists and the next check-in date is set.

items.t: Agent-friendly checkout
items.d: Guest checkout, clear field labels and error messages. Test the checkout with an agent on a test environment.

x.what: AI agents, such as the agent modes in ChatGPT or Claude, can fill in a checkout form the way a person does. An agent-friendly checkout lets customers buy without creating an account, uses clear labels on every field and shows error messages that say exactly what is wrong.
x.why: Agents get stuck on unclear forms, hidden fields and vague errors. If your checkout stops them, they move on to another store that lets them finish the purchase.
x.how: Check that guest checkout works. Review every checkout field for a clear visible label and every error for a specific message. On a test environment, ask an AI agent to buy a product and record where it fails. Fix the problems and repeat. Done when the agent completes a test purchase without help.

items.t: Local payment methods available to agents

x.what: The payment methods your customers use most in your country, such as local bank transfers, mobile payment apps, cards and wallets, can also be used when an AI agent completes the purchase. This depends on your payment provider and on the agent platform.
x.why: An agent finishes a purchase only with a payment method it supports. If your popular local methods are not available to agents, customers in your country may not be able to buy from you through AI.
x.how: List your top payment methods by share of orders. Ask your payment provider which of them it plans to offer for agent purchases and when. Record the answers and track changes. Done when you know the status of each top method and have a date for the next review.

items.t: Product data API with clear access rules
items.d: Price, stock per store, specs, delivery time; authentication, limits and SLO monitoring.

x.what: An API (a way for other systems to request data from yours automatically) that serves product data: price, stock per store, specifications and delivery time. It has clear rules on who can use it, requires a login key, limits how many requests each user can make and is monitored against an SLO, a promised level of speed and uptime.
x.why: Agent shopping protocols such as UCP, ACP and MCP all need fresh product data on request. A stable API is the base for connecting to any of them, and it avoids building a separate solution for each platform.
x.how: With IT, decide which data the API returns and who may use it. Set up authentication, request limits and monitoring. Write short documentation. Test with a sample request for price and stock. Done when the API answers with current data, access needs a key and monitoring alerts on failures.

items.t: Data ready for UCP checkout
items.d: Healthy Merchant Center account, return and delivery policies, OAuth 2.0.

x.what: Google's UCP (a protocol for buying inside AI Mode and Gemini) draws on what you already keep in Merchant Center. This item means the Merchant Center account has no serious errors or warnings, return and delivery policies are filled in, and your system supports OAuth 2.0, a standard way to let another service act on behalf of a logged-in customer.
x.why: When UCP opens in your market, stores with clean data and the required setup can join quickly. Stores with account problems will have to fix them first.
x.how: Open Merchant Center diagnostics and fix all errors and important warnings. Fill in return and delivery policies so they match your site. Ask IT whether customer accounts support OAuth 2.0. Done when diagnostics show no serious problems, both policies are complete and the OAuth answer is documented.

items.t: UCP or ACP prototype on a test environment
items.d: Go or no-go once your market opens.

x.what: A test build of in-chat checkout using UCP (Google) or ACP (the protocol from OpenAI and Stripe), run on a test environment and not on the live store. The goal is to learn how much work it takes and what is missing. Once your market opens, you decide go or no-go based on what you learned.
x.why: A prototype shows the real effort and gaps before there is time pressure. When a platform opens in your country, you can decide quickly instead of starting from zero.
x.how: Choose one protocol. Build a simple prototype on a test environment using the published specification. Write down what worked, what failed and the estimated work for production. Done when the prototype runs a test order and the go or no-go criteria are written down.

items.t: Store MCP server (2027)

x.what: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI assistants connect to a company's data and tools. A store MCP server would let an assistant search your catalogue, check prices and stock, or find a store near the customer. The source plans this for 2027.
x.why: MCP works across many AI assistants, so one connection can serve several of them. It gives assistants direct access to your current data, without guessing from web pages.
x.how: Plan it after the product data API (11.5) is in place, since the MCP server can use that API. Start by deciding which actions to offer, such as product search and stock check. Done for now when it is on the roadmap with a planned date and depends on 11.5.

items.t: Hybrid site search (text plus vectors) with an A/B test

x.what: Search on your own site that combines two methods. Text search finds exact words such as a model name. Vector search, which compares meaning instead of exact words, finds results for questions such as 'small camera for travel videos'. Hybrid search uses both. You test the new search against the old one in an A/B test.
x.why: Customers now type longer, conversational questions, the way they talk to AI assistants. Search that understands meaning helps them find products on your site, and the A/B test shows whether it actually sells more.
x.how: Choose a search tool that supports hybrid search. Run it for part of your visitors as an A/B test against the current search. Compare conversion from search, searches with no results and revenue. Done when the test has a result and you have decided to keep or drop it.

items.t: Internal search logs as a source of questions for 8.5

x.what: Your site search records what visitors type. These logs show real questions and needs in customers' own words, including searches that return no results. This item uses the logs as one source for the bank of customer questions (8.5).
x.why: AI assistants answer the questions people ask. Searches on your own site show which questions your content should answer, so pages built on them have a better chance of matching what customers ask AI.
x.how: Export the most common searches and the searches with no results for the last 3 months. Group them by topic. Add the useful questions to the customer question bank (8.5). Repeat every quarter. Done when the export is part of the question bank process.

items.t: AI assistant on the site, labelled as AI
items.d: AI Act, article 50.

x.what: A chat assistant on your site that answers product questions using AI. The visitor is told clearly that they are talking to AI and not to a person. The EU AI Act, article 50, sets transparency duties for systems that interact with people.
x.why: An assistant on your own site can answer the same conversational questions customers ask ChatGPT, using your current data. Clear labelling keeps you in line with the transparency duty.
x.how: Choose a tool and connect it to your product and policy data. Add a visible label such as 'AI assistant' at the start of every conversation. Check with your lawyer how article 50 applies in your case. Test answers on a set of real questions before launch. Done when it is live, labelled and tested.

items.t: Wrong prices and stock in AI answers kept in check
items.d: Frequent updates (7.3) and checks in the test prompts.

x.what: AI assistants sometimes show an old price or say a product is in stock when it is not. This item keeps that risk small in two ways: your feed, site and structured data are updated often (7.3), and your monthly test prompts check whether AI answers show correct prices and stock.
x.why: A wrong price in an AI answer leads to disappointed customers and complaints when the real price differs. Frequent updates give AI systems fresh data, and regular checks show where errors still appear.
x.how: Confirm that prices and stock update at least daily in feed, site and structured data. In your test prompts, note whether price and stock in each answer are correct. Investigate every wrong answer and trace its source. Done when updates run daily and the prompt check reports price and stock accuracy every month.

items.t: Omnibus: lowest price of the last 30 days on discounts, consistent with feeds
items.d: To confirm with a lawyer.

x.what: The EU Omnibus rules require that when you announce a price reduction, you also show the lowest price from the 30 days before the discount. This item means the price is shown correctly on the site and that the same information is consistent in your product feeds. Whether and how feeds are covered should be confirmed with your lawyer.
x.why: AI systems read prices from your site and feeds. If a discount looks different in the feed than on the page, AI answers may show a misleading discount, which is a legal and trust risk.
x.how: Check with your lawyer what the rules require for your site and feeds in your country. Check 20 discounted products: the lowest 30-day price is shown on the page, and the feed matches the page. Done when the lawyer has confirmed the approach and the sample passes.

items.t: EU warranty label: date and scope agreed with a lawyer
items.d: Prepare the data for 6.9.

x.what: The EU is introducing a harmonised warranty label, a standard notice that tells customers about their legal guarantee and any extra commercial warranty. The start date and scope differ by country. This item means agreeing the date and scope for your country with your lawyer and preparing warranty data for structured data on product pages (6.9).
x.why: Customers often ask AI about warranty terms. Preparing the data now means it can appear correctly in AI answers and you meet the legal duty on time.
x.how: Check with your lawyer when the label applies in your country and what it must contain. Collect warranty data per product or brand: length, type and provider. Plan the template change and the structured data with IT. Done when the date and scope are confirmed in writing and the data is ready for 6.9.

items.t: GDPR: logs with IPs, Consent Mode, no personal data in feeds and Q&A

x.what: Three GDPR points connected with AI work. Server logs used to analyse bot traffic contain IP addresses, which count as personal data. Consent Mode, a Google setting that adjusts tracking to the visitor's consent choice, must be set up correctly. Product feeds and published customer questions and answers must not contain names, emails or other personal data.
x.why: Feeds and Q&A content are sent to Google, Microsoft and AI platforms and may be repeated in AI answers. Personal data in them would spread far beyond your site.
x.how: Check with your lawyer or data protection officer how long logs with IP addresses may be kept and why. Confirm Consent Mode is active and tested. Scan feeds and Q&A content for names, emails and phone numbers. Done when retention is documented, Consent Mode works and the scan finds no personal data.

items.t: AI Act and review of AI-assisted content

x.what: The EU AI Act sets rules for how companies use AI, including transparency in some cases. This item means checking which of your AI uses fall under it, such as a chat assistant, and putting a human review step on content written with AI help, such as product descriptions and guides.
x.why: AI text that nobody checked can contain wrong specifications, and AI systems may repeat those errors to customers. Review protects accuracy, and knowing your AI Act duties avoids legal surprises.
x.how: List where you use AI to create content or talk to customers. Check with your lawyer which AI Act duties apply to each use. Set a rule that a named person checks AI-assisted content before publication. Done when the list exists, the duties are documented and the review rule is in use.

items.t: Image and data licences in feeds
items.d: Plus the conscious decision on training bots (3.3).

x.what: Images and texts in your product feeds often come from manufacturers or photographers. This item means checking that your licences allow sending this material to Google, Microsoft and AI platforms. It also links to the written decision on whether AI training bots may use your content (3.3).
x.why: Feeds go to AI shopping surfaces that show images and text to many people. Material you have no right to share there creates legal risk, and a clear training bot decision shows you chose what happens with your content.
x.how: List the sources of images and texts in your feeds. Check the licence terms of each source for use in third-party platforms, and check with your lawyer if unclear. Remove or replace material without clear rights. Done when every source has a known licence and the training bot decision (3.3) is written down.

items.t: No dependence on a single protocol

x.what: Several protocols compete for agent shopping: Google's UCP, ACP from OpenAI and Stripe, and MCP. This item means you do not build your whole setup around only one of them. Your core data and systems, such as the product data API (11.5), should work with any of them.
x.why: Protocols and programmes change often, and it is not yet clear which will matter in your market. If you tie everything to one, a change in that platform can leave you starting over.
x.how: When planning agent shopping work, check that each piece serves more than one protocol. Keep protocol-specific code in a thin layer on top of shared data. Review the choice every quarter. Done when the architecture plan names a shared data layer and no production checkout is built for a single platform only.

donts: Do not treat llms.txt as the key to AI.
Do not make separate Markdown versions of pages that block Googlebot and Bingbot (cloaking).
Do not look for a special schema for AI and do not add HowTo.
Do not aim at keyword density.
Do not write long descriptions by hand for the whole catalogue.
Do not generate hundreds of pages with AI text without an expert.
Do not block all AI bots with one switch in Cloudflare.
Do not forget that a named bot in robots.txt ignores the * group.
Do not build a production checkout for one AI platform now.
Do not buy another monitoring tool before agreeing a shared setup in the group.
Do not mark reviews from other sites as your own.
Do not put the price in the meta description.
Do not compare KPIs or A/B tests without filtering bot traffic.
